2.title: Why is sleep care hitting a bottleneck?
detailed: Why is sleep care hitting a bottleneck?
Look at the cycle between the Patient, the Physician and the Hospital.
First, Fragmented data: We only get a one-night snapshot.
Second, Hospital reliance: It takes a lot of medical resources and hospital beds.
Third, Patient inconvenience: Patients have to come to the hospital just for the test.
And Treatment blind spots: At home, we can't easily tell if treatment is used, or if it works.

3.title: How do today's tests compare?
detailed: Polysomnography (PSG): scope, All Sleep Diseases; ≥20 wires; wait time 1-2 Months; multi-day, No; Uncomfortable.
Home Sleep Testing (HST): OSA Specific; 3 wires; ~1 Week; multi-day, No; Uncomfortable.
Oximeter: OSA Specific; 1 (Finger); Immediate; multi-day, 7-14 Days; Uncomfortable.
ECG Patch: OSA Specific; 1 (Chest); Immediate; 7-14 Days; Prone to allergy.
To close this gap, we need to move from wearable sensors (Types I/II) to fully non-wearable, continuous monitoring.

4.title: Why is sleep testing so hard?
detailed: Why is sleep testing so hard?
The Waiting Room: If we suspect sleep-disordered breathing, we need objective data.
But getting that data is a real hassle.
The Wired Patient. Clinical Note: sensor application time often exceeds 60 minutes, causing anxiety.
And patients have to sleep in a very unnatural setting.

6.title: Radar principle diagram
detailed: Here is how the radar works.
The Radar sits at a distance, D0, from the User.
It sends a signal from Tx and picks up the reflection at Rx.
A small chest movement, Δx, changes the received pulse.
We see this as the time of flight, ToF, and the phase shift, Δφ.
From these changes we rebuild the breathing, with no wires.

8.title: Our three published studies: sleep lab, home, and heart
detailed: Our three published studies: sleep lab, home, and heart.
The core: a 24-GHz continuous-wave radar plus deep neural decision trees.
Study 1: In the sleep lab (N=196). We compared it directly with gold-standard polysomnography (PSG). Strong correlation (r=0.91).
Study 2: At home (80 patients, 147 nights). Sleep testing at home, with no professional needed to set it up.
Study 3: The heart (N=72). Periodic breathing (PB) picked up by radar was associated with impaired LVEF.

11.title: Airflow defines the event. Radar sees the chest wall.
detailed: Airflow defines the event. Radar sees the chest wall.
Standard scoring and radar look at two different signals.
Standard scoring: airflow. Airflow stops (apnea) or gets shallow (hypopnea).
We only see these events when we measure airflow.
Radar: chest-wall motion. Radar senses the chest rising and falling, not airflow.
If we read chest motion as airflow, we get blind spots.
Blind spot: In an obstructive event, the patient keeps trying to breathe, but no air flows. So chest motion isn't the same as airflow.
Radar has to spot a typical pattern of chest-motion changes.

12.title: How radar sees a sleep-breathing event
detailed: How radar sees a sleep-breathing event: five steps in chest-wall motion.
1, Normal breathing: The chest moves regularly, at normal size.
2, Apnea onset: Movement drops sharply, or stops.
3, Struggling effort: The airway is still closed. The chest makes small moves, trying to breathe.
4, Recovery surge: The airway opens. One big breath as breathing comes back.
5, Back to normal: Movement goes back to normal.
This whole sequence is the event that radar can detect.

15.title: From research to the ward: a zero-contact care platform
detailed: From research to the ward: a zero-contact care platform. We now use the radar every day for our inpatients.
Sleep-Breathing Health Care Platform: Breathing: monitored nonstop, with no contact. Heart rate: read from the same radar signal. Bed status: in bed, out of bed, and moving.
Alerts sent to the care team: Out of bed too long: staff get a reminder when a patient is out of bed too long.
Abnormal vital signs: shown on the ward dashboard. Push notifications: staff get messages on the dashboard and LINE Notify.
National quality recognition: 2021 SNQ, Symbol of National Quality; 2022 NHQA, Distinctive Center – Sleep Center.

38.title: What to take home
detailed: 1. Contactless: A 24-GHz radar can monitor breathing night after night, with nothing to wear.
2. Consistent: It agrees with standard tests in the hospital (r=0.91) and at home (r=0.87).
3. A validated screen: It's TFDA-cleared to screen for suspected severe OSA (bRDI ≥ 30), with 90.5% sensitivity.
4. Looking ahead: We found associations between periodic breathing and cardiac impairment. So it may help us watch the heart, too.
5. Recognition: We received SNQ (2021) and NHQA (2022, 2025) national quality awards.
